speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON REPORT OF SPECIAL MISSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In view of the announcement yesterday of the findings of the special mission to Europe of the national productivity council, to the effect that there were serious gaps in management-labour-government arrangements on economic and social problems in Canada, will the minister say whether he will take immediate steps to bring together responsible representatives of government, labour and management to study the report of the special mission, and to explore measures to be undertaken to deal with these problems?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON REPORT OF SPECIAL MISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been studying these matters for quite some time. We have had several conferences between senior representatives of management and labour, one in Ottawa a year and a half ago and another last spring at Queen's University, both

Inquiries of the Ministry very extensive conferences. My department and the productivity council are working continuously with labour and management to try to bring about the same degree of labour-management-government co-operation-which has proved so effective in the countries of western Europe.

speechtext: A supplementary question. In view of his reply may I ask the minister, who obviously has not read the special report announced yesterday, what steps the government is taking to meet the requests made by the president of the Canadian Labour Congress, Mr. Jodoin, with regard to his membership on the productivity council?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the president of the Canadian Labour Congress chose of his own free will and accord, and for reasons of his own and of his congress, to resign his membership on the productivity council. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a supplementary question. May I ask the minister whether the government has asked the national productivity council to give consideration to putting labour's members on the council on a representation basis, as asked for by Mr. Jodoin?

speechtext:

The Address-Mr. Cashin I therefore call on the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) with the due attention of the house.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my voice to those who have already offered you praise and congratulations on your elevation to your new post. I should also like to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply on their very creditable efforts.
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy and honoured to take part in this traditional debate. I may say that I am particularly honoured because the constituency which I represent in this house was represented for a great many years in the house which presided over the destinies of the then colony, and later dominion, of Newfoundland by my late grandfather, Sir Michael Cashin.
Would that I could continue in such a reminiscent and pleasant vein on this the occasion of my first speech. But, Mr. Speaker, at this time, in this place, and in this country circumstances are such that the members of the house should at all times devote their energies and their attention to the great problems facing this house, and facing indeed the whole nation of Canada. So, Mr. Speaker, I am rising to support the motion of want of confidence placed before the house. If there was any doubt in my mind that I should do so, it was certainly dispelled after enduring the long barrage, indeed the deluge, from the other side of the house. Instead of adopting a straightforward approach which would show that this government appreciates the problems that face the Canadian nation, they have chosen to put on the blinkers that have obscured their vision for so long. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that there was no example in the speech from the throne of the moral fibre and the moral courage which the people of Canada have every right to expect from their government at all times, and particularly at this time. Oh yes, there have been a great many words. Indeed, the manipulation of language seems to be one of the few significant traits of this government that I have been able to observe in the short time I have been here watching the other side of the house. Words that I thought had one meaning to all or most people seemed to have different meanings to suit the occasion for the members on the other side of the house. For example, we heard the very fine sounding phrase that fear begets fear, and indeed it sounds good. It perhaps sounds better than does my phrase that government mismanagement begets government mismanagement and that government befuddlement begets government befuddle-ment.
Another interesting observation is this. While the members on the other side of the

house are entrusted with the responsibility of government and have been entrusted with that responsibility for five years, they can come into this house, as they have done in other houses, and accuse 50 Liberals of obstructing about 200 people from governing Canada. If 50 Liberals could be so successful in doing that, how successful would they be on the other side of the house?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Twenty two years.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Indeed, I am glad to know that those on the other side of the house have not lost their ability to use words. However, I noted that the statements which have been made indicate indeed that the speech from the throne is not what the Canadian people expected. I humbly suggest that otherwise they would have held all of us for, whatever side of the house on which we sit, we are all in the same house. If one group does not live up to its standards, inevitably it affects all of us who are in this profession. I am afraid that is what has happened, namely that they have not given us what they should have given. I humbly suggest that had they done so, they would have been held in higher regard by the people of Canada, instead of indulging in obvious attempts at grasping for straws. They have embarked on a tremendous manhunt to discover what went wrong and who is to blame. I believe it is obvious to the majority of Canadians what went wrong and who is to blame. It must have been a shattering moment to see the house of cards come tumbling in. I suggest that the reason for the great outbursts on the other side of the house and directed at this side of the house and at our leader is based upon the fact that this group is in office but not in power, and that the great shock of it all is not the trouble that faces Canada but the realization that they are not invincible and are subject to mortality. If I were to believe all I have heard quoted from the other side of the house, it would seem that everybody is out of step but them. However, I do not believe that is good enough for the Canadian people.
As hon. members are no doubt aware, I represent a Newfoundland constituency. I should therefore like to devote a goodly portion of my remarks to the constituency and the province which I represent. This constituency and this province have been adversely affected, as have all provinces and all parts of Canada, by the way in which this government has handled itself. However, in this province there are some peculiar and particular problems which are demanding special attention. Indeed, there is another problem down there for the other side which they would like to take care of, but that is

not the one about which I am going to talk. I might remind you, Mr. Speaker, that if Newfoundland, the province which I am proud to represent in this house, is to grow, to develop and to make an increasing contribution to the growth and development of Canada-and by that I mean a contribution commensurate with her capabilities and potential-then there are certain physical and geographical conditions which must be recognized by the federal government by way of action. If you look at a map, you will find that the problem of Newfoundland is obvious. It is a problem of communications. We have an area of 43,000 square miles on the island itself. There are 6,000 miles of coast line, and over 1,000 communities are scattered around this coast line.
Progress has been made. In fact progress was bound to be made because there was nowhere to go but up. It gives me great pleasure as a Newfoundlander to drive into tiny hamlets on roads however dusty, because I know that two, three or four years ago there were no roads. I am deeply moved by the enthusiasm of the people who greet me because of appreciation of what has been done. We all remember that in the 19th century the matter of communication was one of the most significant problems to the fathers of confederation. In fact, even today it still is, although "communication" is perhaps a larger word today. I refer not only to physical communication but communication of ideas. However, communication has been and for a long time will be one of the keys to the success of confederation.
The problem in Newfoundland today has reached the stage perhaps that unless and until the federal government of Canada is prepared to recognize the special and peculiar nature of this problem, then I really do not see how Newfoundlanders can be truly integrated into confederation and can consider themselves to be first class and equal Canadians. It is not the fault of the men who go down to the sea in ships, that this problem exists. Their own government and their own people have made great sacrifices over the years in order that many of these problems may be circumvented. What has been done by the federal government to alleviate this problem? What has been done to show that the federal government appreciates and recognizes this problem as a special and peculiar one demanding particular attention? Of course Newfoundland benefits, as do all provinces, from the arrangements made under the Trans-Canada Highway Act to pay all provinces a certain proportion of the cost of building a trans-Canada highway; but this arrangement still leaves Newfoundland with a much greater relative cost than any other province. It must be remembered that Newfoundland
The Address-Mr. Cashin has enjoyed the advantages of confederation for about 13 years while the rest of Canada has enjoyed these advantages for 95 years.
This past summer there was a so-called opening of a so-called trans-Canada highway and this matter brings me back to my earlier point about words. I do not know what is regarded in some quarters as a highway. However, I know that in Newfoundland in many places we have secondary dirt roads and in other places none. I also know that most of the people I have met from the mainland of Canada and most of the people I have met from the United States regard a highway as something with asphalt on top of it over which human beings in automobiles can drive in relative comfort. When this opening was held I understand from very reliable sources that a good many inquiries were received from people in the United States wishing to come to Canada. They heard that there was now a highway right across Canada but they did not know about the game with words being played in Canada. So they were very much disillusioned when they arrived in Port aux Basques and began their trek across Newfoundland.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I was very disturbed to see no mention of this matter in the speech from the throne. It is plain that the government of Canada is content to have Newfoundland relegated to a lesser position in the confederacy that is Canada. Therefore it is not very difficult to know why the little strength that the Conservative party has had in Newfoundland is diminishing. It is diminishing because the people in the government have not approached the problems of Newfoundland from the point of view of finding a straightforward and equitable solution.
There is much talk about the Canadian economy and about productivity but in Newfoundland I can think of hardly anything that would help our economy more than the trans-Canada highway. It would literally get our economy moving. It was not enough that this very basic problem of Newfoundland was ignored, but in fact we had to endure the embarrassment of politics being played with the word "highway".
I was also saddened to note the absence of any mention of fisheries in the speech from the throne. In fact I believe that the fisheries are a problem of national importance which affects, of course, not only Newfoundland but Quebec, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and British Columbia. It is disheartening for one who comes from an old historic fishing area to see no mention of the fisheries. When I have travelled about my constituency it has been disheartening for

The Address-Mr. Cashin me to learn of the work of foreign trawlers which have ravaged fishermen's gear by coming in to the very headlands of the sea. It was disappointing and made me most sorrowful to learn from the fishermen, who after all live in an area with the highest cost of living of any province and the lowest standard of income, that their gear was being harassed by foreign vessels and, worse still, their traditional inshore fishing grounds were being interfered with by foreign trawlers.
I realize that there has been talk of a 12-mile limit, but from all I can gather it seems that a 12-mile limit will not be realized at all if the attitude of the present government outside of the house is to be believed, or at least it will not be realized in the near future. I believe that the establishment of a 12-mile limit, whether we do it by speeding up negotiations on an international level or by taking the bull by the horns and doing it ourselves, would be a significant step forward for the fisheries not only in Newfoundland but in our sister provinces on the Atlantic coast. It is not enough to tell these fishermen in eastern Canada that a 12-mile limit cannot be established because after all they realize that Iceland, which has less than half the population of Newfoundland, was able to do it. Has Iceland more courage, more moral fibre than Canada?
But mention of the 12-mile limit was not the only omission vis-a-vis fisheries in the speech from the throne. The federal government ought to concern itself more with the policy or idea of putting capital into the fisheries because the fisheries, particularly in Newfoundland, and I realize also in other provinces, have the problem of modernization. Generally speaking, these foreign trawlers that come over and ravage our fishing grounds are far better equipped to approach the fisheries and have an advantage in that regard over our fishermen. There is a real need. I realize that government, be it federal, provincial or whatever the level, cannot take it unto itself to solve all the problems of the fishermen. Indeed, that is not what the fishermen want and anybody who has any experience or knows the fishermen knows that one of their significant traits is their independence of spirit which makes it difficult for them sometimes to accept outside help. They are not looking for handouts; rather, they are looking for a constructive program from the federal government.
Another result of a program to make capital more readily available would be that it would assist men in eastern Canada to get back into the fisheries. In Newfoundland, as in our sister Atlantic provinces, we are confronted with unemployment. We have a very high birth rate in Newfoundland so I suppose that

conceivably we could have more people working one year in Newfoundland and have twice as many unemployed as in the previous year. Evidently the natural increase does not seem to be noticed by the federal government. They have not taken judicial notice of the fact that the human race increases and so when they talk about unemployment and jobs they forget to realize that at least in Newfoundland we are very good at it. Indeed, that is what they fear, that we will become too good at it, populate all over the place and bring our political philosophy with us.
Newfoundland itself has recently called a conference on the fisheries and I think this will mark an improvement. The fact that the federal government knew this was going on in Newfoundland made the omission of anything to do with fisheries all the more striking. I am afraid "statesmanlike" is not the word to describe this omission. I wonder, Mr. Speaker.
We in Newfoundland are a reasonable and fair-minded people and we will support any legislation whatever the source of which is aimed at dealing with our particular and peculiar problems. The first is the problem of communications and the need of roads to open up our country so that we may enjoy confederation the same as all other people can enjoy it and so that our storehouse of wealth may be better cultivated. More movement of our people from one place to the other all over the island will help to get our economy moving. It will create, for example, a greater demand in the public service industries. It will give us a better chance to attract secondary industry.
The second of our great problems is the fisheries. I differentiate between these two problems because the fisheries are a problem that we share with many other provinces. We have peculiarities in our fisheries as they have in theirs. The situation is somewhat like that in agriculture. I cannot emphasize too strongly how very important this problem is in Newfoundland. I am sure it was the intention of those who brought about confederation that both governments would deal with Newfoundland in a spirit of co-operation and show an interest in solving this problem. We do not want to slip into confederation and be forever doomed to the role of second class Canadians. We came in so that we could make a contribution to the success of confederation. Is it to be held against us, Mr. Speaker, that our political philosophy does not happen to coincide with that of the government of the day? We did not expect confederation to be a panacea and now that we are in confederation we do expect that we will be required to pull our weight and to do what we can.

The situation is like an investment. We have already given Canada sovereignty over our immense Labrador which has great mineral resources that are just now beginning to be developed, in addition to the resources of timber, minerals and fisheries on the island and around the island itself. We have also contributed to the confederation a market which it did not have previously and now, of course, we get most of our consumer goods from the mainland. However, we still sell the major portion of our products to foreign countries. That is why we in Newfoundland are particularly worried about some of the things said and done about trade policy on the other side of the chamber. Trade policy is very important for the people of Newfoundland, and its mishandling is another example of how the government has alienated the support it originally had there.
We in Newfoundland were shocked, as were people all across Canada, to see the great about-face that took place so shortly after the election. We were told that there was no crisis before the election; but now I, and other hon. members, are glad to learn that the crisis which did not exist has been cured. There is a lesson to be learned from that by one making his first appearance in parliament, and if this session continues-and there is a mathematical possibility that it might-I suppose I shall learn the English language as it is spoken in this chamber. Of course I must also learn the French language, as it is spoken, but I believe I shall have an easier time with it.
The government has claimed that its record is unequalled. I agree, and only hope that we shall never again see a government in Canada with a record like it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), and other hon. members who have already taken part in this debate, in complimenting the mover and seconder of the speech in reply to the address on the very excellent job they did in making their maiden speeches and moving and seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I feel sure that their constituents are proud of them, that their own families are proud of them, and that those who elected these members as their representatives in Ottawa will feel again very sure that they send excellent representatives to be their members of parliament.

Mr. Speaker, in the short time available to me this afternoon I should like to speak very briefly about the Canadian economy and about some of the things which the government is doing to assist our industrial and trade expansion. Speaking yesterday, the Prime Minister referred to the strong advance which had been made in several of the key indicators in our economy, and he mentioned that the gross national product had been running at record levels. I think hon. members might be interested in hearing the actual figures of this key indicator which measures the strength not only of our economy, but of any economy. The gross national product for the first half of 1962 stood at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $39.1 billion, compared to $36 billion in the same period of 1961. That is an increase of 8.6 per cent. Mr. Speaker, only a small part of this increase was the result of higher prices. The gross national product expressed in terms of constant -that is, 1957 dollars-rose from $33.8 billion to $36.4 billion between the same two periods, which is an increase of 7.7 per cent. This expansion in our productive activity which has taken place during the past year has made it possible, as the Prime Minister so ably pointed out yesterday, for 200,000 more Canadians to be working in August, which is the last month for which figures are available, than were working at this time last year; and I think that those figures I have mentioned are a clear indication that our economy is moving ahead very strongly indeed.
I should like now to mention some of the things that the government is doing to help maintain that expansion. On September 4 the government announced a new phase of our trade expansion program, made up in several parts. The first part is a plan to fly more than 700 important buyers, carefully chosen from all parts of the world, to Canada next spring to inspect the products which Canadians have to sell. Mr. Speaker, not only will these important buyers be able to inspect our products under the most favourable circumstances and, we hope, be able to place a considerable number of orders here at that time but, equally important, they will be able to advise our producers in instances where our products do not measure up to the standards required by them so that they would place an order, of what must be done by our producers in order to get orders in the future.
This was one of the most important phases of the two similar trade shows which were held this spring in Toronto and Montreal. A great many sales were made to important American buyers who came to these cities from Chicago, New York and Philadelphia, 27507-3-Hi
The Address-Mr. Hees which are important buying centres in the United States market. Also, the large number of buyers who went there were able to point out to our producers, and very kindly did so, where they fell down, and for what reason, in certain instances where they were not able to place orders with the Canadian producers. They showed them that if they were able to improve their design in a certain way, to improve their quality in a certain way, or to lower their prices by a certain amount, then they would be able to place orders with them; and this is one of the important things that our Canadian producers learned at those meetings. I have learned since that time that many large and important orders have been made possible through the information passed on to our producers by the buyers who attended those two shows.
The second part of this new activity will be the bringing of our trade commissioners home at this time to Ottawa for a week's conference with myself and the officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce to discuss at first hand, ways and means which we can adopt to enable our producers to sell more actively, effectively and successfully in the markets of the world A similar conference was held, as you know, Mr. Speaker, in this city in December 1960, and very good results were obtained because our trade commissioners who came home at that time were able to discuss at first hand with our officials what could be done in their particular markets; and I would say that in every case their suggestions have been carried out with beneficial results.
The third part of this trade expansion activity will be to invite businessmen from all over Canada to come to Ottawa to meet with our trade commissioners in private session. This will be similar to the meetings which took place here in Ottawa in December 1960, when, as you know, Mr. Speaker, something over 1,350 businessmen from all parts of Canada came to Ottawa, and in more than 10,500 individual half-hour sessions with our trade commissioners from all parts of the world were able to find out at first hand what chances there were for selling their products in the markets in which they were interested. In many cases they found out for the first time that to their great surprise sales could be made of their products in those markets; and since that time they have become firmly established in the export market, their sales have grown year by year, and they are making good sales which have resulted in worth-while increases in employment in their plants. The program which we expect to have carried out here in Ottawa at that time we believe will be about twice the size of the conference that was held in

The Address-Mr. Hees December I960, and at that time the businessmen who come to Ottawa will not only be able to talk with our trade commissions from all around the world, but will be able then to go across the road and talk to our departmental officials in the trade and commerce building, to the great benefit of both.
Then following that, Mr. Speaker, on September 7 the government held here in Ottawa an industrial expansion conference to which were invited over 400 leading industrialists from every part of Canada, who met with senior government officials to discuss the means that we in this country can adopt for promoting additional industrial expansion. In particular, the conference was called to discuss how to bring about the greater use of products, either made in Canada, or which could be made in Canada but which are now being brought into Canada from outside sources. In the morning, papers were presented by six outstanding industrialists: specifically, the president of the Ford Motor Company, the president of the Imperial Oil Company, the president of Du Pont of Canada, the president of Electrohome, vice president of Northern Electric Company, and vice president of the T. Eaton Company. They were chosen to present these papers because already in their company they had made important contributions to the purpose we had in mind, which is specifically the expanding of the use of products which are already made in Canada, or which could be made in Canada, and which are being brought in from outside.
In the afternoon, a wide open discussion was held. I think it was the opinion of all those who attended, both government and businessmen, that a great deal of benefit resulted. Typical of the excellent papers that were presented was the one given by the vice president of Northern Electric Company, who outlined in some detail a plan which his company had been operating for the past six years. This plan entailed the following. They set up a team of engineers who examined more than 10,000 individual products which the company at that time had been importing into Canada for use in their production, in order to see which of these products either could be bought in Canada, or could be produced in Canada. They set themselves two extremely strict criteria. The first was that they would not accept anything inferior to what they had been bringing in from the outside, just because it was Canadian. The second was that they would not pay more for the product just because it was Canadian. Operating on those two extremely tough criteria they found that the result of this operation has been no less than spectacular. Of more than 10,000 products which
[Mr. Hees.l
formerly were imported into Canada by this company, today only 800 are imported, and they are still working on those 800 in order to ascertain which of them can be changed from one category to the other. The remaining more than 9,000 products which they formerly imported, of a total value of $11 million a year, are now manufactured in Canada, and are providing 1,600 steady year round jobs for Canadians to work at. This operation has resulted in a substantial saving to the company, and the tooling costs have been recovered in the first 12 months of production of the new products. I believe we would all agree that this is an excellent example of what can be done to use more products which are now being made in Canada, or to have manufactured in this country products which we are now bringing in from the outside.
Many of those who attended the conference have since told me that they have already started on a program similar to that embarked on by Northern Electric Company six years ago. As a follow-up to this conference, we are going to hold, all across Canada, similar conferences on a regional basis. The purpose is to bring together Canadian producers in all regions of Canada in an effort to try to get as many as possible into this worth-while and important program to produce more products here in this country and to work out the practical details with the practical men concerned at those regional conferences. The first of these regional conferences will be held in Montreal in the first week of November. Other conferences are planned in other parts of Canada in the months ahead. When completed, this program will produce many thousands of additional jobs for Canadians to work at.
Mentioned in the speech from the throne were several measures which were designed to help industry become more competitive, which already appeared in last spring's budget, and which will be presented to parliament for passage at this session. The first of these measures reduces the tax rate by 50 per cent on sales in excess of those made in the previous year. This tax incentive will be a great spur to production. It will make it possible for producers, who up until now, particularly in the export field, have not felt that certain ventures provided sufficient profit margin to make it attractive to enter those export fields. Now, with this production incentive, they will be able to enter those export markets, become established, and produce more sales and jobs for Canada. It will also be a great help to Canadian producers who produce for the home market, to help them to meet stiff competition from products that come into this country from other sources.

The second incentive is one which makes it financially attractive for producers to do more research in our country. This will do several things. First of all, it will help to improve the design and quality of Canadian products, and will help us to do something which we must do if we are to be as successful as we must be in the markets of the world, namely, to produce individual and distinctive Canadian design and qualities which people will ask for by name. Second, it will provide work for our young scientists, who, all too often, come out of university here in our country and drift to other more lucrative jobs in other countries. It is hoped that a great many of these young scientists will now, as a result of this incentive, be able to stay in Canada. The third incentive encourages the exploration and development of our oil and gas resources. The benefits from that policy, of course, are only too obvious.
Also, in the speech from the throne is mentioned a measure to help producers make sales in the export market, namely the proposed amendment to the export credit legislation. This will make it possible for the Export Credit Corporation to handle a great deal more business on terms which will be more beneficial to our customers, and also, thereby, our export business. This export credit legislation, and our export financing legislation which was amended at the last session, has made it possible for many millions of export sales to be made in all parts of the world and which otherwise would not have been possible. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the export credit legislation insures against loss in these foreign sales, and the export financing makes it possible for us to sell capital goods on long term credit; sales which would otherwise be impossible to many countries to which we sell. These policies will be continued, and will be expanded where necessary.
The programs and policies that I have mentioned are, as I have said, aimed at helping industry produce and sell more efficiently and effectively. However, I think it is obvious to all of us, especially those of us who are engaged in business, that the most important effort must come from industry itself. Government can do a great deal to help industry, and government is doing so and we plan to do more. But industry of course-and this is recognized by industrialists-must do a great deal to help themselves.
Today I am glad to say that I sense a new spirit of confidence and competition among businessmen in Canada. Whereas a few years ago Canadians did not think they could compete overseas in many lines, they have now learned they can do so by having these
The Address-Mr. Hees things pointed out to them by our trade commissioners and other people who have been in these markets. They are learning that Canadians can compete successfully in world markets if their product and their price are right. Also, Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, labour, management and government are moving considerably closer together, and are showing a greater willingness to co-operate. As you know, this is extremely important, as it is one of the main reasons why those who compete against us in trade from countries of western Europe are being so successful in their competition against our products. There, labour, management and government sit down at the same table, and in a really co-operative spirit, work out ways and means whereby they can make their products competitive so that they will sell in markets around the world. I think an outstanding example of this new labour-management co-operation was in the excellent railway settlement that took place here in Canada only a short time ago.
Management and labour, travelling together on our trade missions abroad, have seen at first hand how labour and management cooperate in these other countries through which they have travelled, and how this co-operation is making it possible for those competitors of ours to make their products competitive and thereby sell and provide jobs.
Our trade commissioners abroad can do a great deal to help Canadian producers sell their products in the markets of the world. They tell us that Canadians have a great reservoir of good will in all the markets they serve; but these foreign buyers want to see us visit their markets in person; bring our products with us; get to know these buyers; discuss our products with them; and make the sale on the spot. They tell us that if our products are competitive in quality, design, price, service and delivery, we will get a break on almost every occasion, because these people like doing business with Canadians. They like doing business in dollars. They like doing business with people who live up to their word, as Canadians do, and whom they can trust in a contract. Generally, for many reasons, they like doing business with Canadians, and therefore we should make the best use of this very real advantage that we have. But, as I have said, our people must be willing to go abroad and make contacts and sales.
If our products are competitive, they will sell, and thus create jobs. If they are not competitive; if they are passed over; then they will not create jobs, and they will not create profits. The people of western Europe and Japan have learned that only too well. It is up to Canadians to realize that more

The Address-Mr. Hees than they appear willing to realize it at the present time. I believe and I am confident, Mr. Speaker, that if we are willing to work as hard with our brains and with our hands as our competitors are willing to work with their brains and their hands, we can have any level of employment in this country that we are willing to work for.
The government, as I have tried to outline in this house on many occasions, has a great many services available free of charge to business, to be used by these businesses to help them produce better for the domestic market, and to get into the export market, no matter what size they are, and sell with success, to enlarge their sales, to enlarge their runs, to get their costs down, make more sales, and create more jobs. But there is just so much that we can do if they do not get in touch with us. I appeal to every member of the house to go to the producers in his area and tell them that if they are interested in developing small businesses, or making small businesses bigger, they should get in touch with us and tell us what their problems are. We have answers to almost any problem they have got. We are not miracle men, but we have people who have made studies in practically every line of business, and we can be of assistance to businessmen, no matter what the size of their businesses. We can help them produce more efficiently, we can help them produce more effectively, but they must get in touch with us. Please have them get in touch with us so we can be of use to them at no cost to them whatever.
We can help them to get into the export market, no matter what size they are, if they have a product that is a good product or if they are willing to work to make it a better product. We can tell them what they have got to do to make sales abroad, what they have got to do to produce a product of better quality, design, price and so on. We can help them, but we want them to let us know they are interested. Help will then be readily available and will come forward in a very short time, a period of time which may surprise them.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say that at this particular time when the world is a very competitive place indeed, when new market arrangements are developing; when the general movement appears to be toward a lowering of tariffs; when businesses have got to stand more and more on their own feet; it is up to Canadians in every line of economic endeavour to get to work to bring their costs down and to get their quality and design up, so they can stand on their own feet, and so they can expand in this tough, competitive world. We have a great challenge facing us today, as has every

country in the world, because there is a limited market and a great many people competing for it. Nobody is going to buy our products just because they are Canadian. They are going to buy only if they are the best quality and the best price.
I am convinced that Canadians can produce products that are better, and can be sold more cheaply than those of anybody else in the world. I am not willing to accept as a fact that we cannot. This government is ready and willing, as it is doing day by day with people who are coming to see us, to help people to produce better and sell their products more effectively and more widely. I am convinced, as I say, that if we are all willing to work hard to make our products competitive, and if we are willing to go out to the markets of the world and sell our products aggressively, we can enable this country to reach its full economic potential. Mr. Speaker, it is up to us.

The Address-Mr. Argue

We say this government should have a policy with regard to railway line abandonment-that the people who built their farms and businesses along those branch lines which will be affected should not suddenly find that as a result of a simple declaration the lines are to be torn up and the value of their properties sharply decreased. We believe there should be a policy as a result of which anything which is necessary in this respect may be done in an orderly fashion; that there should be policies to cushion some of the financial loss which is bound to result. The effects of such a policy will not be confined to any one part of Canada. I began by saying I did not feel the agricultural producers were asking for special consideration. Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate my first words must be of congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They have acquitted themselves well. Their families and their constituents have every right to be 27507-3-124
The Address-Mr. MacRae proud of them, and we can see a great future for them in this house. I should like too to congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, on your elevation to the office which you hold. Your record in peace and in war is known to all of us, and we wish you many years of success in your position. To you, sir, now occupying the chair we extend our congratulations and our best wishes; your reputation for fairness and common sense is well known to all of us.
Mr. Speaker, I will be brief because I know there are many who wish to take part in this debate. Many years ago it was said to me that there are four primary duties of a member of parliament. First, he should press for those measures which are in the national interest. Second, having done that he should work for those measures which are in the interests of his region, of his province, and of his constituency. Third, if he is a party man, as we in this country who adhere to the party system are, he should support his party; he should be loyal to his party. Finally, it is his duty, having served, to be re-elected. I do not intend to discuss in the short time at my disposal the last two of these, but I should like first of all to talk about those measures in the speech from the throne which are of interest to all of us nationally, then, the matters of interest to those of us who come from the beautiful province of New Brunswick; and lastly, matters of interest to me in my own constituency of York-Sunbury.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that every one in this house regardless of party should compliment our government on the program of legislation which is envisaged in the speech from the throne, and on the action which is intended through that legislation. I would especially like to commend for his address to this house the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees). President Kennedy a short time ago said of the United States of America that they either had to "trade or fade". The Americans use many of these catch phrases, but this one, it seems to me, is very apt. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has brought to his department a dynamic approach, and the steps which he listed this afternoon will go far in keeping Canada in its rightful place in the world.
Another measure in which I was interested, which was discussed in the speech from the throne, was the royal commission on taxation which is now sitting. As one interested in small business, I feel that our government should take the lead in reducing taxes. We are now taxed too much. Taxes after a while tend to become a burden and to stifle industry. I was especially pleased to note that this commission is soon to report.

The Address-Mr. MacRae
The last speaker mentioned the unemployment insurance fund in connection with another group which he thought might be brought under this particular fund. I believe, and I think all sound-thinking Canadians believe, that something will have to be done in the near future about the tremendous number of abuses which are taking place under this fund, abuses which were never envisaged when the fund was set up. Also, the proposal to set up a national welfare council was mentioned in the speech. I have never agreed with the principle that voters should be bribed through welfare payments. I think that we in this country have now reached the limit in welfare payments beyond which it is not safe or wise to go. I was pleased to see that in the speech from the throne there were no handouts. True, some people-and this was proven in the last election-are bribed at times by such promises, but surely the majority of right-thinking Canadians will see these promises for what they are worth.
There were two other measures of interest to me. I believe that contributory pensions are a most worth-while step. If people are shown that they do not get anything for nothing in this world but must pay for everything, then I believe they will accept and support this measure. Contributory pensions will make it possible for people to set aside amounts under some well defined plan for their old age to supplement what governments can provide. Also, there was the question of portability of pensions. I realize that this is a provincial matter, but I would urge our government to take every possible action to encourage the provinces to help bring this about. Unlike some who are economists, perhaps, I get a little bewildered on occasion with monetary funds, devaluation, and matters like that, but there is one thing about which I have no doubt at all. As far as devaluation is concerned, we in the maritimes have had the best tourist season in the history of that part of Canada, and I am sure that will also apply to all parts of our nation. For that we can thank devaluation.
I have another item I wish to discuss which is of great interest to me, that is, that we should give consideration to the establishment of a national office of education. True, under the British North America Act each province has its own system of education, and, of course, Quebec has two. That was necessary in times past, but times have changed. In the old days it took many weeks to get across our great nation. Now we can cross it in a few hours. Families are moving about. In my constituency we have Camp Gagetown, and there are several thousand soldiers there with their families. A few years ago I was told that one

family had moved five times in one year, and they had children. Hon. members can see what that would do to the education of these children. I think that it is time that we gave some thought to standardizing education across this nation, and I believe it will come, with, of course, the co-operation of the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, I have reason to believe that the next point will be touchy to many hon. members. It was mentioned in the speech from the throne that consideration would be given to the question of a Canadian flag. As far as I am concerned there will be no other flag that I will support except the red ensign. That was the flag under which I fought during the last war. It was good enough for those who came before me, and I am satisfied with it.
Those were the national measures about which I wanted to speak. Now I should like to talk for a moment or two about matters of provincial and constituency interest. When I came here a few years ago, a very fine member of the House of Commons represented the constituency of Fort William. He had been here for many years. After I had been here about a month or so, he took the occasion one day to walk across the floor of the house to this side to talk to two or three of us. He said to us: "Young fellows,"-I was rather complimented by that-"you will find that there will be so many things going on here that you won't be able to keep track of them all. I suggest to you that you pick out three or four of more interest to you than anything else, get to know all about them, and press for them on every possible occasion. In that way you can make your greatest contribution to this house". On thinking that over, I decided that my objective would be to support in every possible way those measures which would raise the economy of our Atlantic areas of Canada, our maritime provinces.
The history of the maritimes is well known. It is said that England suffers from too much history; but we in Canada suffer from too much geography. We in the maritime provinces are an example for the second part of that statement. We suffer because we are so far away from the central part of Canada. We know that in 1864, when the maritime provinces were talking of union. Sir John A. Macdonald came to Charlottetown. He persuaded those meeting there to go to Quebec, to give up the idea of a maritime union, and to join in the formation of the Dominion of Canada. We did that, of course. On the first day of July in 1867, the Dominion of Canada came into being. However, we gave up a great deal in the maritime provinces when we went in with Upper and Lower Canada and formed this nation. Our trade had been with the New

England states, in the days of the wooden ships and iron men. Some have said to me that it might have been better if we had joined the United States in those years. Perhaps we would have been better off. On the other hand, perhaps we would not. At any rate, over the years our people have had to leave the maritime provinces. They have gone out to the rest of the nation and they have gone to the United States to head universities and great business establishments. That is the sort of thing that went on for nearly 90 years until in 1957 there came into office in this country a government which had a new concept of the problems of the maritime provinces. I refer to such matters as adjustment grants, aid to power development and all those other things.
Finally, in the speech from the throne there is the proposal to establish an Atlantic development board. I should like in a moment to quote a short editorial which sums up this matter very well. It is sometimes said that it is all right for you fellows in the Atlantic provinces to be complaining all the time, but what are you yourselves doing about this matter? We are trying to do something, Mr. Speaker. We are trying to raise ourselves by our bootstraps. An example is the Atlantic provinces economic council formed eight years ago and now composed of 1,800 able businessmen, university leaders and so on in the maritime provinces. They are trying by every means at their disposal to encourage industry, by research and development, to raise further the whole level of Atlantic Canada.
I believe that the solution of our problem in the maritime provinces-and certainly in my own province of New Brunswick-lies in the establishment of small industries which will employ 10, 20, 50 or 100 men and based on our natural resources. The experience has been that if one big industry closes, a whole section of our region can be vitally affected, as illustrated by the difficulties in the coal producing areas of Nova Scotia. We, of course, know of these difficulties and we sympathize with these people of Nova Scotia who are having them. However, there is not very much that can be done about the matter. We know that today coal is not being burned. We know that oil is taking its place. We realize the difficulty in the lumbering industry because of automation. Years ago logs were being cut by means of the saw and the use of men's strength. Then the chain saw was invented. It could do in one day what eight men did previously. Now there is a machine that will go through the forest and harvest logs like a mowing machine going through a field of
The Address-Mr. MacRae hay. To my mind, small industries are the answer to our economic difficulties in Atlantic Canada today.
Now, I should like to quote briefly from an editorial which appeared in the daily Gleaner of September 28, 1962, and in which the Atlantic development board is mentioned. It states as follows:
The great news for maritimers in the speech from the throne is, of course, the Atlantic development board announcement. This is what the people of the Atlantic provinces have been fighting for over the past years. It signifies the realization of our hopes and the fulfilment of our aims.
The Atlantic development board will be the means of implementing the pledges inherent in the Atlantic resolutions. In announcing in the mari-times his intention to establish it, Mr. Diefenbaker coupled it with the Chignecto canal and tidal power development. He said then that he hoped the proposal for the Chignecto canal would be the first project brought before the board, and that the board would also complete the power studies ...
Here at last-
In the words of the editorialist of this great champion of Atlantic development,
-is the means at hand to end the injustice that has cursed the regional economy for a century.
It has been said, Mr. Speaker, that we as Conservatives have not obtained the best press over the last few years. Perhaps that is so. If it is so, perhaps in many cases it has been our own fault. I believe that if Canadians are fully informed about the steps which this government is planning and which are envisaged in the speech from the throne- and by the way, I feel that the press has been giving excellent coverage to it during this past week-they will commend and accept them and will support this Conservative government in the steps which it plans to take in the years ahead.

Mr. Speaker, in congratulating you upon the very important office to which you have been appointed and in congratulating Mr. Deputy Speaker I should like to apologize for any part that I have had in this slight confusion between the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) and myself. I should also like to congratulate hon. members opposite who moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. As a new member

speaking for the first time in this house I can say with great sincerity that I thought they performed their tasks very well indeed.
I feel deeply honoured, Mr. Speaker, to be here, a new member of this house, as the representative of Davenport riding in Toronto. I follow in the footsteps of two men who served that riding faithfully and well, Mr. Douglas Morton from 1957 to 1962 and my friend, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), who was the member for Davenport from 1949 to 1957. Both these gentlemen have many friends in the riding and I shall hope to live up to the standards they have set.
Davenport is typical of the changing city of Toronto. Probably a majority of the residents of that riding were born there or have lived there for a long time; but in addition there are a great many others who have come to Canada since the war. Many of these people have language problems and thousands of them have not yet obtained their Canadian citizenship. These newcomers are unfamiliar with our ways and they should be given special attention and special help with their problems. Many of these newcomers are making a very great contribution to the life of Canada and to the life of Toronto. In Toronto their presence is being felt in the professions, in business, in politics, in the arts and in the art of living. Toronto is a more pleasant place in which to live than it used to be, and to a large extent this is due to the influence these new Canadians are having.
One of the changes, Mr. Speaker, is that the term "Tory Toronto" no longer has any meaning in that city, except perhaps in an historical sense. I expect that 16 of 19 members from the Toronto Yorks and Peel constituencies will agree with me when I say this, and we hope to do better next time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: Particularly in Eglinton.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Davenport, as I say, is typical of this new Toronto; and its people, its residents, have the same problems and the same fears as many hundreds of thousands of other people in urban centres all through this country.
The first of these is unemployment and the fear of unemployment. This is the No. 1 problem for this parliament to deal with and I for one was not impressed with the rosy optimism and the questionable statistics expressed in the speech from the throne on this score. If anybody would like to go to Davenport or to any other of the similar ridings in Toronto he will find plenty of unemployment now, and the fear that there will be a great deal more unemployment before this winter is over.

In addition to this fear of unemployment, there is a great need in these urban centres particularly, although I think it applies to all ridings throughout Canada, for more action and more help in the field of social security. There is a clear need for a national health plan.

Anyway, Mr. Speaker, I am not too interested in what was needed in the past. I am interested in what is needed now and what must be done. I for one place a national health plan very high on the list and I place it with the need for more adequate provision being made for our older citizens. I include in this proper housing for those older citizens as well as adequate pensions. I think people are more conscious than they ever were of the need for improvements in our educational system, and I include in that vocational and training programs. These are things that concern not only the people of Davenport but people in most parts of Canada these days.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
